title: Gratitude: It Does a Family Good
author: John McLean
summary: In issue 31 of Wisdom From Dad, John McLean uses his memories of Thanksgiving and the after-dinner walks his grandfather took him on, each beginning with the question of what he was thankful for, to argue that gratitude is a practice fathers can build into family life. He observes that ambitious men are so focused on the next promotion or deal that they miss the gifts in front of them, and he contrasts taking each day 'as granted' with taking it 'for granted'. The week's tenet, accept gratefully, does not ask a man to pretend a setback is fine; it asks him to see that failures shaped him as much as successes did, and that he can be grateful and still ambitious. McLean notes that several religious traditions converge on thanksgiving and then gives a simple two-part routine: write ten gratitudes on a notepad at night and begin the morning with a spoken thank-you. He ends with the fatherhood point, that children are watching how their dad handles disappointment and what he appreciates, so one simple question at the dinner table may stay with them for decades.
points: Gratitude is a habit of attention that ambitious men must choose deliberately, because a focus only on what is next hides what is already given.
Take each day 'as granted' rather than 'for granted' and treat setbacks as formative, without abandoning ambition.
A two-part practice works: one minute of handwritten gratitudes before bed and a spoken thank-you on waking.
Fathers teach by example, so thanking your wife, appreciating who your children are becoming and handling disappointment well are the real curriculum.
One simple recurring question, such as what are you thankful for, can become a tradition that outlasts the dad who asked it.
quotes: When you are in the trenches, like most ambitious men are, it’s hard to see the gifts that are constantly being laid at your feet. Your eyes are on the next promotion, the next big deal, or even the next job.
When you shift your perspective and learn to take each day and each experience as granted rather than for granted, it opens the door to all sorts of possibilities.
Think about this. The setbacks you’d rather forget helped to make you who you are today. They’re every bit as important as your successes.
You can be grateful for what you have and still be ambitious about what you want.

You don’t need a turkey in the oven, or four generations gathered around a beautifully set table to give thanks. Life doesn’t have to meet your expectations before you can express gratitude for what you have.
Our families don’t need us to have all the answers. They need us to be present, to appreciate what we have, and to show them by example what it means to live a good life.
That’s the thing about being a dad. You don’t always know which moments your kids will remember, or which of your habits and traditions they’ll carry into their own lives.
